title: BMW Teases A New Street Bike – Could It Be the F 450 R? - Motoroids
content: Earlier this year in the month of April, BMW Motorrad launched the much awaited F 450 GS in India. It was a topic of discussion for a long time. Now the brand has teased a new naked streetfighter motorcycle, which is expected to be a naked sibling of the F 450 GS. BMW has not officially confirmed the name yet, but the motorcycle appears to use the same new 450 platform. The global unveiling is scheduled for October 1, 2026. The teaser shows a compact motorcycle with a sporty shape. The fuel tank looks large and muscular, while the front section gets a sharp design. The motorcycle also appears to have an upright riding position, wide handlebar and USD front fork. The F 450 R name is expected because BMW already uses the F 450 GS name for its adventure motorcycle. However, the company is yet to confirm the final name. The new motorcycle is expected to use the 420cc twin cylinder engine from the F 450 GS. BMW lists this engine with 48 hp and 43 Nm of torque in the GS. It uses a six speed gearbox and has a 135 degree crankpin offset. BMW could make changes to the engine tuning for the streetfighter. The gearing and throttle response may also be different, although these details have not been confirmed yet. The F 450 GS also gets BMW’s Easy Ride Clutch as an option on selected equipment. It is not known if the same system will be offered on the new roadster. The F 450 GS uses long travel suspension with 180mm travel at both ends. The roadster is expected to get a shorter and more road focused suspension setup. A lower seat height is also possible, but BMW has not shared these details yet. The motorcycle is also expected to have a steel frame related to the 450 platform. The teaser suggests a smaller rear section, raised pillion seat and a sporty tail. BMW Motorrad will reveal the new motorcycle on October 1, 2026. Its India launch date has not been announced yet. Reports suggest that the motorcycle could be priced around Rs 4.5 lakh if launched in India. The possible rivals include the Aprilia Tuono 457 and other motorcycles in the 400cc to 500cc street bike segment. More details about the engine tuning, equipment, dimensions, price and India launch should be known after the global debut. For now, BMW has only shown a teaser, while the F 450 R name and most technical details are still expected information.

title: The Motorcycle We'd Choose For A Ride Across All 50 States - Top Speed
content: Subscribe to the TopSpeed newsletter to never miss an update Riding through all fifty American states is an epic, life-changing cross-country marathon that is filled with changing horizons and local characters. Thanks to the vast network of high-speed freeways, it's quite comfortable to cover 48 of the 50 states (the contiguous U.S.). But to enjoy the journey and explore all fifty states, with unforgettable hidden gems along the way, you have to embrace the roads less traveled. What better way to do that than to pick a go-anywhere adventure tourer that can tackle anything thrown its way? A flagship BMW ADV tourer tops this list with adaptive underpinnings, a relentless engine, and one of the biggest fuel tanks on a motorcycle. The beauty of America shines when you ride through all 50 states. From highways, parkways, country roads, forest service roads, urban alleys, and gorgeous mountain passes and coastal roads, America has a lot to offer. For those who want an endurance run through most of the states, they can choose high-speed, multi-lane interstate highways with controlled access. A motivating example is Brock Gill, an avid rider who undertook a fast-paced challenge to visit all fifty states in fifty days, covering over 13,000 miles on a Triumph Scrambler 1200 XE. Many more riders undertake longer, multi-year 48-state rides to explore hidden spots in each state. The challenging part comes when riders leave popular roads behind and take rural and remote roads, including forest service roads where reception is also limited. But these challenging routes are also the most rewarding for soaking up America's beauty. Mountain passes with dramatic drop-offs, steep grades, and unpaved roads challenge riders to use their skills to the fullest. Examples include the Beartooth Pass in Montana/Wyoming, rural Alaska, and the Great Plains. Saving Alaska or Hawaii for last dials up the sense of true achievement, as dramatic, towering peaks and hanging glaciers add to the emotional impact. Instinctively, we assume baggers and full dressers are the best touring choices for exploring all of America. Traditional, low-slung touring bikes tick most boxes with a torquey engine, heavy-duty, stretched-out underpinnings, a low-slung design with accessible seat heights, and solid wind protection. Standard weatherproof saddlebags and top boxes (in the case of a full dresser) easily provide storage for two. Prime examples include the Harley-Davidson Road Glide / Street Glide, the Indian Roadmaster, the BMW K 1600 lineup, and the Honda Gold Wing / Tour. But these long-standing touring bikes have one problem: a lack of versatility. They perform exceptionally on tarmac but become a burden when riders steer off onto gravel and dirt. Downsides include low ground clearance, less suspension travel, restricted maneuverability, and weight. The goal of the newer wave of flagship adventure touring bikes is to eliminate these shortcomings while still upholding the American touring dream, delivering strong performance on both tarmac and gravel. The BMW R 1300 GS Adventure takes the spotlight by adding more mile-munching features, including a gigantic fuel tank bigger than any Harley or Indian tourer to date. Starting at $23,795, the R 1300 GS is a great globetrotter and the perfect companion for exploring all of America because BMW designed it from the ground up for transcontinental travel. Its legacy began as a mash-up of off-road and touring motorcycle parts on the iconic R 80 G/S. Years of evolution have made the GS nameplate the flagship adventure touring bike that can conquer it all. The R 1300 GS's predecessor—the R 1250 GS—was quite capable, but it had size and weight-distribution issues. They weren't major, but they were enough to hamper a balanced riding experience. Things obviously got dialed up on the R 1250 GSA, which carried more weight. With the R 1300 GS, BMW is rectifying these core problems. The standard ADV has been re-engineered to carry its weight better, deliver power more linearly, and maintain its all-around capabilities, especially off-road. The touring-focused R 1300 GSA adds versatility with a huge fuel tank, more durable standard cross-spoke wheels, and slightly longer suspension travel. Also, it comes with BMW's Dynamic Suspension Adjustment as standard. The GSA is also more rugged, with standard heavy-duty engine protection bars. It is also better prepared for the unknown with features like integrated auxiliary lighting, integrated luggage mounts, and comfort features like heated seats. An evolved boxer-twin engine powers the R 1300 GS Adventure. The 1,300 cc mill is liquid-cooled, has four valves per cylinder, and a 13.3:1 compression ratio. Its ShiftCam variable valve timing technology on the intake valves greatly contributes to this engine's versatility and performance reserve across the rev-band. The R 1300 GSA produces 145 horsepower at 7,750 RPM and 110 pound-feet of torque at 6,500 RPM. That makes it the most powerful BMW adventure bike on sale today. Despite its heft, this Beamer can easily breach 120 mph. Power is sent to the rear wheel via a six-speed manual gearbox and a final low-maintenance shaft drive system. While the standard six-speed with an assist and slipper clutch is good, BMW's optional Automated Shift Assist adds a new layer of riding simplicity. It uses the same six-speed gearbox but eliminates the need to operate the clutch when shifting or when starting and stopping. This add-on is a great help, especially when maneuvering this beastly ADV along challenging mountain passes with steep inclines and declines, or even through tight city traffic. This is thanks to its huge 7.9-gallon fuel tank, which is the largest on any touring motorcycle. For reference, the most capable American tourers, like the Harley-Davidson Grand American Touring models, have a 6.6-gallon fuel tank. Indian Motorcycles like the Challenger and Pursuit have a smaller six-gallon tank. Even the most popular and tech-savvy metric tourer—the Honda Gold Wing—has a relatively smaller 5.5-gallon fuel tank. Interestingly, the closest touring rival in fuel tank size to the R 1300 GSA is another Beamer—the K 1600 series of touring bikes, with a fuel capacity of seven gallons. The nearly eight-gallon fuel tank makes the R 1300 GSA an ADV that can easily do 350 miles between gas stops. The R 1300 GSA sits on a unique diamond frame that uses the boxer-twin as a stressed member. It features a heavy-duty bolt-on sub-frame designed to handle the added load of a pillion and luggage. BMW's patented Duolever and Paralever setup handles suspension duties at the front and rear, respectively. The front comprises a wishbone layout and an internal spring. The rear gets a single-sided swingarm with a monoshock. As mentioned before, the GSA offers slightly more suspension travel than the standard R 1300 GS model with 8.3 inches up front and 8.7 inches at the rear. Its 593-pound curb weight makes the suspension setup impressive and helps it tackle rough trails with confidence. Braking duties are taken care of by twin 310 mm semi-floating front discs coupled to radial four-piston calipers. The rear gets a 285 mm disc coupled to a two-piston floating caliper. The standard model sits on 19-inch front and 17-inch rear tubeless spoke wheels with radial all-purpose tires. A tall and adjustable windscreen, adjustable seat height (34.6 inches to 35.4 inches), comfortable seat materials, and an adaptive rider triangle all support comfort and riding dynamics on the R 1300 GSA. Other features that make this cross-country companion more comfortable include heated grips, heated seats, and adaptive cruise control. The cockpit features a sizable 6.5-inch TFT display with Bluetooth and integrated navigation. The standard feature list is comprehensive, including keyless ignition, a tire pressure monitoring system, auxiliary lights, and an auto-leveling electronic suspension. A six-axis IMU and by-wire throttle help this Beamer seamlessly integrate a stacked suite of safety and assistive features. Notable ones include four riding modes (three more with the Riding Modes Pro package), dynamic traction control, engine drag torque control, linked braking, cornering ABS, and hill hold control. The optional technology list is more exciting but also demands a serious premium. Notable features include adaptive vehicle height control and the aforementioned automated shift assistant. It also gets a radar package that enables active cruise control, front collision warning, lane change warning, and rear-end collision warning. The option list often drives prices up because BMW doesn't allow individual add-ons, and most of the best features are locked behind packages, the most affordable of which is the Racing Red Package, starting at $3,845. Despite the sticker shock from optional packages, the BMW R 1300 GS Adventure is still worth it for being a go-anywhere ADV that doesn't compromise. It redefines exploration and endurance without sacrificing comfort, convenience, or luxury. Its seasoned yet evolved boxer-twin engine, unique yet durable underpinnings, and loaded technology features make the biggest BMW adventure bike the most durable one for exploring all of America. title: Why Markets May Be Pricing in Too Many Fed Rate Hikes - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. Markets may be pricing in more tightening by the Federal Reserve than is warranted due to a divergence playing out in the economy, according to Goldman Sachs Vice Chairman and former Dallas Fed President Rob Kaplan. In the Goldman Sachs Exchanges podcast, Kaplan notes that while artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure and defense spending are continuing to boom, interest-rate sensitive parts of the economy, such as housing and autos, are already straining under higher rates. Taken together, these crosscurrents are creating a more muted response from the Fed. Allison Nathan: The Fed has just raised interest rates for the first time in three years. So, was one increase enough to bring inflation down, or should investors expect more rate hikes ahead? I'm Allison Nathan, and this is Goldman Sachs Exchanges. Today, we're unpacking what this shift means for companies, for interest rates, and for confidence in the Fed with Goldman Sachs vice chairman and former Dallas Fed president, Robert Kaplan. Rob, welcome back to Exchanges. Allison Nathan: A treat to have you actually in the studio this time around. Allison Nathan: So, as I just said, we have seen the first hike from the Fed in a number of years under new chairman Kevin Warsh. Start off, what was your first reaction to that? Did you think that was the right move? Rob Kaplan: I did think it was the right move. Remember the Fed did three cuts in the fall of 2025. I would not have done the third cut. They were worried about the labor market. We then get into 2026, we've got tax incentives, we've got an AI infrastructure boom, and then you've got the war with an oil spike. I think the Fed tried to be patient, tried to see if oil prices were going to settle back down. They haven't. And so, I think they were right to do nothing in July, but I did believe that September was the time to act, and they did the right thing to raise rates in September. Allison Nathan: But let me just ask you a follow-up because did they do the right thing because of inflation concerns or because the market was so convinced it was going to hike that it didn't really have a choice and is there a difference between those two? Rob Kaplan: Yeah, they had a choice. When you're sitting inside the Fed, I always think I have a choice. And if I think the market is way off, I can go out and communicate and give feedback to the market. But the problem was month-over-month, year-over-year inflation we know is problematic, i.e. it's in the mid threes, but part of that is oil prices a year ago were in the 60s. They're now close to $100, so that's not a shock. The thing that was problematic is the month-over-month numbers. I think they were hoping that those would cool and start to approach, say, 0.2 a month, so a annualized 2.5%, let's say. And unfortunately, they ran hotter than that. So even month-over-month, we're still running closer to three. And I think once they saw that, I believe that it was the right thing to do to start taking action. Now, the issue is how many times do they need to move? And I think the dot plot, interestingly, was pretty muted, showed a pretty muted response, meaning they're going to raise in September. I think the median was one more increase, and then some thought they needed to do a little bit more than that, but I think the median showed they don't take any action in 2027. I would call that a fairly muted response. And the reason it's muted is the AI infrastructure part of the economy, and AI adoption part of the economy is booming. There's no question about that. Defense spending, for obvious reasons, is very strong. However, when you look at autos, housing-related, companies that sell to low, moderate-income consumers, business isn't terrible, but it's pretty sluggish or weak. So, the interest-sensitive parts of the market that are affected by the Fed funds rate are already, in my opinion, not overheated. And so, these crosscurrents sort of created a more muted response from the Fed. Allison Nathan: Right. So, if you think about the fact that nine of the ten officials are expecting at least one more hike, is that realistic, or are you saying they need to actually hike more? Cause the market thinks they're going to market thinks they're going to hike more. Rob Kaplan: The market is anticipating that they're going to hike more and if I were on the committee, my mindset would be, let's move in September. I would probably be inclined, unless there's a reason to act in October, I'd be inclined to skip October. We'll see if they do. And then look again about moving again in December. Then I want to take a fresh look and see whether or not we need to do more. The reason two moves resonates with me, that gets you to four, four and a quarter. They're at three and three quarters to four right now. I know Kevin Warsh said he doesn't use the neutral rate, doesn't look at it, but and I agree with him. It's not the be-all, end-all, but it's also, in my opinion, not irrelevant. I think the neutral rate for me is probably plus or minus one, one and a quarter real plus the inflation rate. I think the nominal neutral rate is around four, four and a quarter. So then the question once, if they raise it again in December, we're then at four, four and a quarter. I'm probably in the neighborhood of neutral. Maybe I need to do one more to be slightly restrictive, but I don't know that I need to do a lot more than that. And the reason, again, I don't know is interest-sensitive parts of the economy are not overheating. And so, I'm sensitive to the fact that the one tool I have, the Fed funds rate is potent, but it's not going to slow down the AI infrastructure build. It's not going to slow down defense spending. And I'm also aware that we've got this oil shock that maybe gets resolved. I don't know that it will, but if it got resolved, that would also cause me to rethink, and I'm aware of that and mindful of it. Allison Nathan: Right. So, just to be perfectly clear, you think the market is pricing in too many hikes at this point? Rob Kaplan: I think the market is yes, expecting more hikes than at the moment, at the moment I think is likely. It's putting in effect, a risk premium maybe for a few factors. So, what could those factors be? One, maybe they say, "I don't understand yet the reaction function of Kevin Warsh and therefore of the Fed, and so I want to build in some cushion." They may also be building in the fact that maybe we can't find a way to resolve the war in Iran, and oil prices stay elevated for much longer than everybody thinks, in which case the curve may be more likely to be higher, and the probability that the oil price bleeds into 30 or 40 items increases. And I think the market's pricing in some risk premium that that could happen. Allison Nathan: Understood. When you think about that decision, what does it tell us about whether the Fed is making decisions without political pressure? We've talked about this in the past. There were some question marks about the Fed's independence with Chairman Warsh coming in. How confident should markets be in the Fed at this point in its independence and the process around. Rob Kaplan: I'm extremely confident that the folks around the FOMC table are doing their level best without political considerations or political influence. They're doing their level best to make their best decision. And so, they're not being swayed by political factors. I think that's true of the participants on the committee. I think people also want to believe that about Chair Warsh, and I think Chair Warsh wants to demonstrate that. I think the raising rates in September was a positive move forward for him in that regard. It shows he's willing to raise rates, but I think the market is still scrutinizing him a bit. But I can tell you around that table, politics or political pressure is not entering into their decision-making. Allison Nathan: Got it. Let's talk about the real economy. We obviously have seen this big move up in Treasury yields across the curve, really. The 10-year Treasury is now above 5%. What are the implications in terms of borrowing costs for companies? You talked about the resilience and strength of the AI. Rob Kaplan: Well, let's talk about the curve. Let's talk about long duration bonds—10 years and longer, even five years and longer. But certainly 10 years or longer are more affected by the national deficit. I think there's a concern there was a hope that if we grew at four to 5.5% nominal this year, which is what we're growing. We're growing two and a fraction real, and inflation's running, you pick the number, 2.5%, 3%. We're running at close to 5% nominal. I think the thought was earlier in the year, if growth was that high, we're going to bend the curve of the deficit. According to the Congressional Budget Office, they've now revised up their estimates, and it looks like the deficit's going to be higher, not lower than it was last year. So then the question is, why? I think that was a little jarring and makes people think maybe government spending either on defense or the war in Iran or other things is much higher than we realize, and it's probably causing the market to be a little bit more discouraged that we've got a grip. And then the second thing is there hasn't been any fiscal plan announced. There have been bond buybacks announced, but I think the market reaction is that isn't going to solve the problem. It might buy you some time or mitigate it on the margin, but there hasn't been a fiscal plan, and so that's affecting the back end of the curve. Oil prices being higher has affected the whole curve. And the irony of the situation is the most booming parts of the economy, in particular the AI boom is being done with debt and in some cases equity along the yield curve, and that's already priced in I think more rate increases maybe even than the Fed's going to do. So that's why you notice the Fed increase rates didn't really have much of an effect on the curve because the curve had already adjusted. So what the Fed is doing really isn't going to slow down the AI build. The people that I talk to that are being affected are people that borrow at the Fed funds rate and that can be small business, it may be some individuals, it'll be some interest rate-sensitive sectors. And I talk to housing companies who are struggling to sell to customers because of high mortgage rates, but they finance their inventory based on short-term debt. So, they're getting squeezed. And so again, a lot of the interest rate-sensitive parts of the economy will get somewhat squeezed by this. Allison Nathan: But corporate CEOs are not so concerned about the rate hikes. Rob Kaplan: They are much more focused on being able to issue equity or on the treasury curve, and I would say credit spreads and the treasury curve have been reasonably well behaved and have already adjusted up, maybe even more than in anticipation of what the Fed is going to do. Allison Nathan: Interesting. We've talked, and you just mentioned a few minutes ago, about transparency around the Fed's process and reaction function, and that has been a big topic in recent months. What are you seeing in that regard at this point, and how concerned are you, or is that really not a concern of yours? Allison Nathan: About transparency around it, that the markets feel less knowledgeable about how the Fed is going respond to data. Rob Kaplan: My advice to listeners would be the following: if you listen to the speeches of Fed presidents and the governors, I think those are very true to exactly what they're saying in the room around the table. Obviously, the chair is being more careful about talking frequently, and he's moderating, he's refining his message. But I actually think if you read Fed speeches from the FOMC participants, you got a pretty good feel on the debate around the table. And so I think there's pretty, actually, I still think there's pretty good transparency. There's a little bit of question, again, trying to interpret Kevin Warsh. The one other thing that I didn't mention that's related to all this is, and you may have heard me say this before, they're very aware at the Fed the share of GDP going to profit for companies is going up. AI is accelerating that, okay? The share going to labor is more muted. And so that's the other reason why you've got more resiliency among companies, in that the prospects for their margins and corporate profits to improve is increasing. The prospects for low moderate-income workers, if you don't own financial assets, yeah, they're getting gains in labor, but they're struggling to make ends meet. And so that's a little also in the back of the minds of people around the table. Allison Nathan: So, but how much is that a problem for the Fed versus a problem for the administration and the fiscal side? Rob Kaplan: It is a issue for the Fed to be aware of because that's a somewhat different dynamic. They're used to at the Fed for the last number of decades, with a few exceptions, you look, is the labor market overheating? Are number of hours worked expanding or decreasing? What happened to real wages? And normally, if the unemployment rate were going down and you saw those other variables improving, you would be worried maybe we're overheating and we need to cool it off by raising the Fed funds rate. I think you've got a low fire, low hire labor market. You've got a different dynamic here where the labor market is not guiding the Fed right now. I think this is a infrastructure boom with a supply shock, tariffs, constrained labor, and oil. That's a different kind of setup. And that's why they're wrestling with how to understand it and how to correctly respond to it. Allison Nathan: One more question for you related to that, which is there's been a lot of focus on supply shocks being more difficult for the Fed to address and navigate. What are the implications for Fed policymakers here? Rob Kaplan: So let's talk about what a supply shock is, and I'll give you my own, my own two cents on it. If you have a supply shock and it lasts for two months, then I think the knee-jerk reaction if you're at the Fed is, "Let's just wait and do nothing, and we'll look through it." If you have a supply shock, on the other hand, that goes on for six, seven, eight months and maybe it could go on for a lot longer, what happens is it begins to bleed into 30 or 40 items, and then a year or two later you forget how the inflation even started. So that's why those who say supply shock, what can a Fed funds rate increase do about it? Well, one thing it can do is prevent the bleed or slow the bleed to 30 or 40 other items. And Warsh even commented on that, and he was right to do it in the press conference. We can't stop the oil shock, but we can slow down maybe the transmission to other items. And I do think they've realized at this point they need to be focused on doing that. Allison Nathan: And it's not just the duration of supply shocks, right? It is the frequency of them, because we obviously had the big COVID supply shock. We have this energy shock now. Rob Kaplan: And I hate to say tariffs is a supply shock, lack of labor force growth, immigration curtailment is another supply shock. We've got a few supply shocks in the face of a historic CapEx boom, and so that's a set of factors that…I'm not sure there's a textbook you read on how to understand how to deal with that. Allison Nathan: Right. Last question for you, Rob. We have another Fed meeting coming up, as we were discussing, in about, let's say, five weeks time. I mean, what will you be watching to give you more confidence in your view that they won't move in October? And what would convince you that they will? Rob Kaplan: So, as always, they'll look at the data. But the other thing they need to be doing, which is we do naturally here and I do in my job at Goldman,  they need to be out talking to businesses. And I will tell you, businesses are telling me again that if it's interest rate sensitive, it's okay, not great, but they need to be out there and understanding what's going on. They'll also get a PCE, a price indicator on, I believe, September 30th, and they'll get a CPI in mid-October. They'll watch both of those. My own view is I would prefer to do this gradually because of the mixed factors I talked about and wait till December. But if those readings or my sense from talking to contacts is inflation is firming, accelerating, or the CPI or the PCE are worse than I expected, that's what might tip them to say, "You know what? We better act in October." Allison Nathan: Thanks very much, Rob. Always a pleasure talking to you. Allison Nathan: This episode of Goldman Sachs Exchanges was recorded on Tuesday, September 22nd, 2026. 				We use vendors that may also process your information to help provide our services. Karol G is riding high. She became the first Latina artist to headline Coachella back in April, her seven Latin Grammy nominations last week tied Rosalía, Jorge Drexler, and Ca7riel & Paco Amoroso for the most among artists, and her highly anticipated album No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto remains in the Top 20 of the Billboard charts — firmly establishing the Colombian superstar in the cultural conversation and positioning her for a historical Grammy run. She dropped No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto on Aug. 7, and the album became an instant hit. It debuted at No. 8 on the Billboard 200 and currently sits at No. 11. While the album was expected to achieve widespread success, following the performances of previous projects Tropicoqueta and Mañana Será Bonito, what was less predictable was the massive response to one particular track: "Bby Wow." The party anthem did not receive the same level of promotion as other songs on the album. It was not released as a single and does not have an official music video, unlike the song "Still," and didn't have as much prerelease buzz as her collaborations with globally popular artists, notably "Ahí" with Drake, "Still" with Bruno Mars, and "Después de Ti" with Greg González of Sleeping With Sirens. While those collabs gained visibility and secured strong chart positions, none has matched the success of "Bby Wow." So far, the song has earned more than 161 million streams on Spotify, remained at No. 1 on Spotify Global since Aug. 28, and recently reached the Top 10 of the Billboard Hot 100. It also surpassed Ella Langley's ubiquitous "Choosin’ Texas" on the U.S. Apple Music chart and reached No. 1 on the Billboard Global 200. The collaboration with Spanish singers Judeline and Rusowsky demonstrates that when a song connects with an audience, the artists’ existing levels of fame do not necessarily determine its impact. The track has also benefited Judeline and Rusowsky, giving the emerging artists greater visibility and expanding their reach in the English-language music industry. Karol G has continued to demonstrate an ability to recognize new talent, giving rising artists a platform and highlighting her commitment to creating opportunities for new voices in music. With all of that in mind, "Bby Wow" has emerged as the potential front-runner for the Grammys’ new Best Latin Song category, with one big caveat. Gold Derby has been unable to confirm whether Karol G’s team submitted the track before the Recording Academy’s deadline. Although the album was released Aug. 7, the song didn't really achieve its breakthrough until the week of Aug. 28, which was the final day for artists to enter music for Grammy consideration. That means there's a chance her team might hold off on submitting the track until the next awards cycle, which could prove challenging, since it relies on voters having long memories. If "Bby Wow" isn't in contention this year, Karol G's team could instead prioritize her Latin Grammy-nominated hit "Coleccionando Heridas" from Tropicoqueta (as Gold Derby predicted back in July) or the new album’s lead single, "Matadora." In any case, Karol G will definitely be on the shortlist of viable artists for Best Latin Song, alongside fellow Latin Grammy nominees Rosalía, Silvana Estrada, and Jorge Drexler. title: Isaiah Rodgers Named NFC Special Teams Player of the Week for Week 2 - Minnesota Vikings
content:
EAGAN, Minn. — Isaiah Rodgers was involved in two game-defining plays. On the first Sunday in Chicago, he dove on a fumble at the goal line, forced by Jalen Redmond, that kept the Bears out of the end zone in the third quarter, then did the "Hot Dog, Hot Dog, Hot Diggity Dog" dance to fulfill a promise to his son. On the second, he zoomed off the edge with six-and-a-half minutes left and rejected a 23-yard field goal attempt by Cairo Santos. The play preserved a 6-3 lead on the way to Minnesota's 9-3 win. It also earned Rodgers NFC Special Teams Player of the Week honors, the NFL announced Wednesday. The cornerback won his first career POTW accolade 364 days ago when he was named the NFC Defensive Player of the Week for his performance of epic proportions in a 2025 Week 3 blowout of Cincinnati. In this instance, he made a brilliant impact on defense, recovering the fumble that turned the tide amidst the slosh at Soldier Field — but his block sent him over the top. In response, Minnesota's offense marched 11 plays, tying its longest possession (by number of plays) of the game and returned the ball after another Will Reichard field goal with 1:09 on the clock. Vikings Special Teams Coordinator Matt Daniels gave his thoughts on the moment Tuesday and listed a number of impressive aspects: Rodgers' ability to eliminate the space between him and the holder; his skill at dodging or knocking down the arm of the "wing" on the end of the line of scrimmage (rookie tight end Sam Roush on this occasion); his preparation and expertise of the opponent's operation; and, of course, his ball get-off in slippery conditions. "Everyone knows that this guy is probably one of the fastest guys in the NFL, but his acceleration to get off of the football and be able to bend," Daniels said. "His ability to slip Roush's hand that got thrown out and be able to bend and be able to take it off the foot — [it] says a lot about the type of athlete that he is, and on plays like that we say it all the time that 'Great plays are made from great effort,' and it was just unbelievable effort by him." Rodgers has done this before for the Purple. He blocked a 30-yard try by Pittsburgh's Chris Boswell, who is close to automatic on kicks under 40 yards in his career (94.6%) during the Ireland game last season. And Rodgers has stated his plans to do it again — and again. "He's already kind of put it out in the air that he's going to take three; he's going to take three off the foot this year," Daniels shared that Rodgers expressed that intention right before the game vs. Green Bay. "That's surely enough the first thing he said when he came to the sidelines [this Sunday], 'That's one Hat, that's one. I got two more to go this year,' so we're off to a good start there." Rodgers got a hand on Santos' 50-yarder on Chicago's opening drive, as well. View game action photos from the Vikings Week 2 game vs. the Bears at Soldier Field. "His pinky wasn't big enough, I guess, to deflect it enough," Daniels quipped. But his near block early on likely affected Chicago's failure to launch later. The sight of Rodgers lined up in a track stance and threatening his speed, at this point, is a warning. "Absolutely," Daniels said opposing kickers are thinking about a possible block. "100%." On Daniels' watch, the Vikings have done a fabulous job of instilling that fear. While opponents have attempted the second-most field goals against Minnesota since 2022 (160), they've converted only 83.1%. That's the 10th lowest hit rate in the NFL in that span, following the Browns (79.1%), Bears (79.3%), 49ers (81.1%), Buccaneers (81.3%), Giants (81.5%), Raiders (82%), Seahawks (82.7%), Patriots (82.9%) and Chargers (83%). Santos has suffered the second-most blocked field goals (five) during that timeframe, by the way. Who has more? title: Can AI Investment Drive S&P 500 Earnings Even Higher? - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. The recent strength of S&P 500 earnings has raised concerns among some investors that stocks are in an “earnings bubble,” according to Goldman Sachs Research. Our strategists expect the boost to earnings from investment in artificial intelligence (AI) to gradually fade, making productivity gains from AI increasingly important for stock profitability. Recent earnings growth has been “extraordinary,” writes Ben Snider, chief US equity strategist at Goldman Sachs Research, in a report. S&P 500 earnings per share (EPS) grew 51% in the second quarter (year over year) and 26% during the past four quarters. By comparison, the S&P 500’s four-quarter growth in EPS has averaged 7% during the past 30 years. Earnings have also pulled ahead of their historical relationship with US economic growth. “Our base case is for S&P 500 earnings growth to decelerate, not collapse, in coming years,” says Snider. “Because equity prices have failed to keep pace with surging earnings, near-term valuations show no hint of a bubble,” Snider writes. The forward price-to-earnings ratio has fallen from 23 times a year ago to 19 times today, matching its 10-year average. That said, “even an 'average' multiple may be expensive if current earnings are unsustainable,” he adds. The cyclically adjusted P/E ratio, which uses the trailing 10 years of earnings, has climbed to one of the highest readings on record. It falls short of the 1999-2000 peak but exceeds the level reached in 2021. Goldman Sachs Research forecasts the S&P 500 will rise to 8,700 over 12 months, up from 7,764 on September 21. Our strategists’ outlook implies a P/E multiple on consensus forward EPS that remains close to the current level of 19 times. Snider expects investors to remain uncertain in the coming quarters about AI’s impact on long-term profits, making a dramatic increase in valuations unlikely. S&P 500 EPS are forecast to grow about 11% in both 2027 (to $415) and 2028 ($460). Earnings are expected to be driven by solid GDP growth and a fading tailwind from AI investment that gradually transitions into a growing boost from AI productivity. “Energy prices and interest rates create near-term macro risks around these forecasts, but the impact of AI is the biggest long-term question for corporate earnings,” Snider writes. Almost half of S&P 500 growth in EPS in 2026 comes from AI investment, according to Goldman Sachs Research. The largest US hyperscaler companies are on track to spend $800 billion on capital expenditures this year, an increase of 94% over 2025. That money is flowing through the earnings of chipmakers, tech hardware suppliers, industrial firms, and utilities, Snider says. There are second-order effects too. The boom has lifted capital markets activity and supported consumer spending through rising household wealth. However, both consensus and Goldman Sachs Research analyst forecasts show hyperscaler capex growing at a slower rate in coming years. In the meantime, the hyperscalers’ equipment carries depreciation charges that keep climbing as spending growth slows. This will further dampen the boost of AI investment spending to S&P 500 earnings growth. “Hyperscaler capex has consistently surprised relative to consensus estimates during the last few years, and the potential for additional surprises going forward creates a wide range of potential S&P 500 earnings outcomes,” Snider writes. Goldman Sachs Research’s equity analysts expect $1.2 trillion of hyperscaler capex in 2027 and $1.4 trillion in 2028. A surprise of $250 billion in either direction next year would move S&P 500 earnings growth by roughly 6 percentage points in the same direction, according to Goldman Sachs Research. Strong demand and tight supply have boosted semiconductor prices and gross margins. Memory producers are generating gross margins of roughly 80%, more than double their historical average. “Margin expansion has accounted for a large share of recent semiconductor earnings growth, but that boost should fade going forward,” Snider writes. The appreciation in equity investment stakes is also temporarily inflating S&P 500 earnings, according to Goldman Sachs Research. Large technology companies recorded roughly $150 billion of unrealized investment gains in private companies in the second quarter of 2026, translating to 12% of S&P 500 EPS. Goldman Sachs Research expects more of this income in the second half of 2026, followed by a much smaller contribution in 2027. title: Fire 90-82 Valkyries (Sep 22, 2026) Game Recap - ESPN
content: PORTLAND, Ore. -- — Carla Leite made the tiebreaking basket with 1:57 left in overtime and then converted a three-point play with 26.5 seconds to play as the Portland Fire ended the season with a 90-82 victory over the Golden State Valkyries on Tuesday night. Leite finished with 18 points for the Fire (17-27), who snapped a four-game losing streak. Bridget Carleton led the Fire with 26 points, including five 3-pointers. Gabby Williams had 17 points for Golden State (31-12), which led 17-0 but had its six-game winning streak snapped. The loss clinched the No. 1 seed in the playoffs for the Minnesota Lynx. The teams traded free throws and 3-pointers to open overtime before Leite's layup gave the Fire an 84-82 lead. Kaila Charles missed a 3-point attempt for the Valkyries before Leite's step-back 20-foot jumper and free throw put Portland up 87-82. The Fire made free throws the rest of the way for the final margin. Tiffany Hayes' 3-pointer gave Golden State a 75-68 with 2:13 left in regulation. Portland closed the gap on a pair of layups from Carleton and Megan DiLeo, and Leite's driving layup and free throw pulled Portland ahead 77-75. Williams' layup tied it at 77 but she missed an off-balance jumper to send the game to overtime. Carleton hit a 3-pointer with 3:20 left in the first quarter to stop the Valkyries' game-opening run. Golden State led 24-10 at the end of the first quarter. Portland clawed back into the game, closing the margin to 29-26 after DiLeo's layup and free throw. DiLeo added another layup and free throw to tie the game at 35 with 33 seconds left in the first half. The Valkyries closed out the half with a 40-37 lead. The teams wrestled for the lead in the third quarter but Golden State held a 61-58 advantage going into the fourth. Valkyries: Visit Los Angeles on Thursday, the final day of the regular season.

Team Germany (Men’s) and Team Europe (Women’s) won the 10th BMW Motorrad International GS Trophy, held in Romania September 13-18. The qualifying rounds did not include the USA this year; however, two Americans qualified through the open International Qualifier, held at Enduro Park Hechlingen in Germany last year. Representing the USA on Team International were Stephanie Townsend in the Women’s division and Jordan Wiley in Men’s. This year’s edition was more technical than ever, with narrow forest trails, washed-out mountain paths, riverbeds and high-altitude routes. After six days and approximately 930 miles, Team Germany (Fabi Fenner, Norman Pleissner, Flo Thomann) won the Men’s competition with 203 points, while Team Europe (Chrissie Harcourt and Anja Filak) won the Women’s competition with 200 points. The Women’s competition was decided only in the final challenge, with Colorado’s Townsend and teammate Eduarda “Duda” Mikulski from Brazil on Team International entering the final day ahead of Team Europe by just two points. “We were certainly the smallest team in the competition,” Anja Filak, Team Europe, said. “But we rode like one body, as one unit. Chrissie is amazing. She gave me a lot of advice, and I was able to follow her and make it through. I gained more confidence because I knew I could follow her and stay focused. I took everything she told me over these days very much to heart and tried to put every piece of advice into practice – and it worked!” “I can hardly describe this feeling,” Chrissie Harcourt, Team Europe, said. “My head is a little all over the place; everything feels a bit shaky. It will take a while for it to truly sink in. I am incredibly proud of both of us.” Shifting weather and a midday downpour made for treacherous conditions for the final 75-mile loop and grassy hillclimbs through the narrow mountain ridges and the “Maze,” a technical obstacle course enclosed by ribbons. In the end, Team Europe secured a narrow victory over Team International. With the podium finish, Townsend cements her place in the history books as the highest-placing American woman in the event’s history. The men’s Team International placed seventh. title: Learnings from Earnings - Goldman Sachs Asset Management
content:
The second-quarter earnings season was one of the strongest in recent years. Adjusted S&P 500 earnings growth reached 32% year-over-year, supported by continued strength in AI infrastructure spending. Positive surprises were exceptionally broad, with more than 85% of companies exceeding earnings expectations and roughly 70% surpassing revenue forecasts.1 Strength extended beyond AI-related infrastructure beneficiaries and into consumer, industrial, infrastructure, healthcare, and technology-related end markets. Worldwide, we have witnessed one of the strongest earnings seasons in recent history. The robustness has been rooted in fundamental earnings delivery rather than expanding market multiples, reflecting healthy corporate profitability across regions. Across major indices, returns were largely driven by earnings growth as many of these markets experienced valuation contractions over the quarter. The strongest returns over the last year have come from Japan, Asia Pacific, and emerging markets, where earnings growth, rather than valuation expansion, accounted for the majority of shareholder returns. With the cost of capital remaining structurally higher, earnings growth is increasingly becoming the primary driver of returns across markets. Source: Factset, Datastream, STOXX, Goldman Sachs Global Investment Research. As of August 31, 2026. For illustrative purposes only. What we believe stood out this season was not simply the magnitude of earnings growth, but its breadth. In the US, adjusted earnings growth exceeded 30%, revenue growth accelerated to its strongest pace in four years, and the vast majority of companies delivered earnings and revenue ahead of expectations. Importantly, strength extended well beyond a handful of AI beneficiaries, with healthy demand evident across consumer, industrial, infrastructure, and technology-related end markets. Management teams consistently pointed to accelerating AI investment, resilient consumer spending, improving margins, and continued investment in cloud infrastructure, power, and industrial modernization. While AI remains an important growth engine, the broader takeaway was that earnings growth is becoming increasingly widespread across sectors and geographies. As company-specific execution plays a larger role in differentiating potential winners from losers, we believe the environment is becoming increasingly favorable for active stock selection. We believe one of the biggest lessons from this earnings season is that execution increasingly matters more than sector exposure. Across industries, earnings outcomes varied meaningfully among companies operating in the same markets. Product launches, pricing, capital allocation, operational discipline, and management execution repeatedly emerged as key differentiators. Healthcare provided one of the most compelling examples. Despite negative sector earnings growth, many companies exceeded expectations through robust commercial execution, improving demand trends, and successful product adoption. Similar patterns emerged across consumer sectors, where market share gains were increasingly driven by company-specific initiatives rather than broad-based improvements in demand. In our view, this growing dispersion reinforces a compelling backdrop for active management. As earnings outcomes become increasingly company-specific, fundamental research and stock selection may matter more than broad sector allocations. This year, we have witnessed single stock volatility far outpacing broader index volatility. For much of the past two years, many investors have focused on the scale of AI-related capital expenditures. This earnings season, the conversation increasingly shifted toward returns. While still early, management commentary provided growing evidence that AI investment is translating into potentially faster revenue growth, stronger customer engagement, and expanding business opportunities. The clearest evidence came from the hyperscalers, where cloud revenue growth accelerated despite difficult comparisons. Collectively, the three largest cloud providers are generating nearly $400 billion of annualized revenue, up 43% year-over-year, supported by continued enterprise demand for AI workloads.2 Demand visibility remained strong, with meaningful backlog growth suggesting customers are making long-duration commitments to expanding AI capabilities. Source: Company reports, Bloomberg. As of July 31, 2026. For illustrative purposes only. Profitability remained resilient despite rising investment. Cloud margins were stable-to-higher even as capital spending increased, reinforcing confidence in the returns generated by AI infrastructure. Beyond the hyperscalers, results highlighted continued strength across the broader AI ecosystem, including cooling, power, semiconductor materials, industrial gases, and data center infrastructure. In our view, the debate is evolving from how much companies are spending on AI to how effectively they are monetizing those investments. As we look ahead, the key message from this earnings season is not simply that results were strong, but that earnings growth is becoming broader and increasingly company-specific. In an environment where execution, competitive positioning, and innovation are driving a larger share of performance dispersion, we believe fundamental research and active stock selection remain as important as they have been in many years. 1 Bloomberg. As of September 3, 2026.
